# Results — Study 441 (Camarilla Pivots)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **the
Camarilla reversal levels L3/H3 are support/resistance the market respects** — tested as a clean
intraday event study: per session compute the Camarilla ladder from the **prior** day's H/L/C,
find the **first** 5-minute bar that touches L3 (long) or H3 (short), enter the **next** bar
(one-bar lag), hold 12 bars (~1h), and measure the reversion **toward the central pivot**. The
honest benchmark is a **random control line** at the same distance from the open. Offline &
deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance **5-minute** intraday bars (price-only, `auto_adjust=False`) — 5 very liquid names: SPY, QQQ, AAPL, MSFT, NVDA |
| Window | **2026-03-30 → 2026-06-23** (As-of 2026-06-24; the in-progress final session **dropped**) |
| Sessions | **59** RTH sessions per name (Yahoo caps 5m history at ~60 calendar days) |
| Events | **363** L3/H3 first-touch events over **289** name-days |
| Control | **27,442** random control-line reversions (matched distance from the open) |
| Rule / lag / costs | first touch → enter **next bar** (one-bar lag), hold **12 bars** (~1h), no overnight carry; **2 bps** one-way spread × 2 (round trip) |
| Fingerprint | `36705730ed53` (sha1[:12] of the five close series) |

> **Short-span & capacity caveat (loud).** Free intraday history is tiny — ~60 days of 5-minute
> bars, ~59 sessions/name. That is a **thin power budget**, so we pool across names, use an
> event-clustered **HAC** *t*, and lean on the random-control placebo. **Capacity is moot**:
> there is no gross edge to scale, and these are already the tightest-spread names available.
> Intraday levels usually die to the spread — here there is nothing for the spread to kill.

## The signal — L3/H3 first-touch reversion toward the pivot

Positive = the level was respected (price moved back toward the central pivot). The one-sample
*t* is on the per-event reversion vs 0; the **HAC** *t* is Newey-West on the daily-mean series
(events cluster within a day and across names on market-wide moves).

| metric | value |
|---|--:|
| pooled reversion (gross) | **−0.017%** per touch |
| one-sample *t* | **−0.44** |
| HAC (Newey-West) *t* | **−2.59** (significant — but **wrong sign**: mild *continuation*, not reversion) |
| hit-rate ("reverted toward pivot") | **48.2%** (below the 50% coin flip) |

The headline number is a rounding error and, if anything, slightly negative. The HAC *t* of
−2.59 is "significant" only in the sense that price tends to keep going *past* a touched level —
the **opposite** of the support/resistance claim. There is no respect-the-level edge.

## The decisive test — does the magic line beat a random line?

The honest test is not "does price revert after a touch?" (a volatile price wandering into *any*
horizontal line banks a little mean-reversion-by-geometry) but "does L3/H3 revert **more than a
random line** at the same distance?"

| | reversion |
|---|--:|
| Camarilla L3/H3 (real) | **−0.017%** |
| random control lines (matched distance) | **+0.250%** |
| real − control | **−0.267%** |
| bootstrap P[level beats random] | **0.000** |

The random control reverts **better** than the "magic" levels. Essentially the entire bootstrap
of the difference sits left of zero: there is **no** sense in which L3/H3 outperform a line drawn
at random. **"The line is special" is busted.**

## Costs — there is nothing for the spread to eat

| | reversion per touch |
|---|--:|
| gross | −0.017% |
| net of 2 bps round-trip | **−0.057%** |

Already ~zero gross; net of a modest 2 bps round-trip it is **−0.057%** per touch — on the most
liquid names with the tightest spreads. No version of the trade pays.

## Robustness — nowhere to hide

**Hold-bars sweep** (the reversion never lifts off zero; the 2-hour hold drifts *more* negative):

| hold | n | reversion | *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 6 bars (~30m) | 363 | −0.022% | −0.72 |
| 12 bars (~1h) | 363 | −0.017% | −0.44 |
| 24 bars (~2h) | 358 | −0.091% | −1.85 |

**By level** — L3 +0.019% (*t* 0.32, hit 54%), H3 −0.047% (*t* −0.92, hit 44%): neither side
clears the bar. **Per name** — SPY +0.032% (*t* 0.96), QQQ −0.027% (−0.52), AAPL −0.062%
(−0.84), MSFT −0.006% (−0.06), NVDA −0.026% (−0.19): no name carries a signal; the best (SPY) is
comfortably inside noise.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful

On a deterministic intraday panel where we **plant** a genuine pull back to the pivot whenever
price passes L3/H3, the test behaves exactly as it must:

| planted respect | events | reversion | one-sample *t* | HAC *t* | hit | real − control | diff *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.0** (no respect) | 51 | −0.032% | −0.59 | −1.15 | 51% | −0.151% | 0.998 |
| **0.5** (strong planted) | 69 | +0.214% | **+6.86** | **+11.94** | 80% | **+0.084%** | **0.003** |

With **no** planted respect the test sits at *t* ≈ 0 and loses to its control (no false
positive); a strong planted pull explodes to *t* = 6.86 (HAC 11.94), 80% hit-rate, and **beats**
the random twin (diff p = 0.003). The machinery detects a real level when one exists — it finds
nothing on the real tape because there is nothing.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** L3/H3 first-touch reversion is **−0.017%** (one-sample *t* = −0.44,
  hit-rate 48%); the HAC *t* of −2.59 is significant only with the **wrong sign** (mild
  continuation). No respect-the-level edge on the real tape. *(Short-span caveat: ~59
  sessions/name — but the random control already beats the real level, so more data is unlikely
  to rescue it.)*
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Net of a 2 bps round-trip it is **−0.057%** per touch on the
  tightest-spread names available. There is no gross edge to scale.
- **"The line is special"? — BUSTED.** Random control lines at matched distance revert
  **+0.250%**, *more* than L3/H3 (real − control = **−0.267%**, P[level beats random] ≈ 0). The
  Camarilla ladder is arithmetic on yesterday's range; the synthetic control proves the test
  would catch a genuine level if one existed.
